claims.statement: All eight concrete action classes (CategoryAction, PropertyAction, ProductAction, ProductImageAction, PropertyValueAction, OrderAction, UserAction, ForeAction) extend Action4Result, which is the only class in the action package carrying @Namespace("/"), @ParentPackage("basicstruts") and the @Results block; no concrete action repeats any of those annotations.

The six-class chain splits action responsibility by member kind: Action4Upload owns img/imgFileName/imgContentType, Action4Pagination owns page, Action4Pojo owns nine entity properties and ten list properties, Action4Service owns the nine @Autowired services plus t2p and saveWithJpg, Action4Parameter owns nine loose scalar fields, and Action4Result owns only routing metadata with an empty class body.

The chain exists because of the README's action-layer refactor: a single CategoryAction had accumulated seven unrelated concerns (page-result definitions, single-object getters/setters, collection getters/setters, the paging object, the upload object, service injection, access-path mapping), which the refactor moved into one dedicated class each, leaving the concrete class with only its endpoint bodies.

The action package declares exactly 47 @Action endpoints: ForeAction 24, CategoryAction 5, PropertyAction 5, ProductAction 5, ProductImageAction 3, PropertyValueAction 2, OrderAction 2 and UserAction 1, while src/struts.xml declares no <action>, <result>, <global-results> or <include> element, so every URL exists only as an annotation string.

The single @Results block on Action4Result holds 36 result names - 26 plain dispatcher forwards and 10 type="redirect" results - and action methods return only the name string, so the view behind any endpoint is changed in that shared block rather than in the action method.

The two URL families follow different naming rules: the 23 back-office endpoints are admin_ + the uncapitalized entity class simple name + _ + the method name (which is why ProductImage and PropertyValue appear as camelCase URL segments), while ForeAction holds all 24 storefront endpoints under a single glued fore prefix with no entity segmentation and no separator.

The endpoint URL and the Java method name are independent: the storefront URL forereview is implemented by the method ForeAction.revice(), and the /fore auth gate keys on the request URI rather than on the method name.

The bindable request-parameter surface is declared only on the chain classes (Action4Pojo's nine entities and ten lists, Action4Pagination's page, Action4Parameter's nine scalars, Action4Upload's three upload properties) and is shared by all 47 endpoints, so adding a parameter means adding a field plus a public setter to one of those classes and a rename there affects every endpoint at once.

t2p(Object) rebinds an id-only bound entity to its persistent row in four reflection steps: read the id via the entity's public getId(), fetch the row through the single type-agnostic categoryService.get(clazz, id), resolve the setter by name as "set" + the entity's simple name on the runtime action class, and invoke it on this so the action field itself is replaced rather than the caller's argument.

t2p()'s contract depends on naming, not types: the entity must expose a public getId() whose value autoboxes to Integer, and the action property must be named set<EntitySimpleName>, which is why its usable arguments are the nine Action4Pojo entity properties and why renaming either side silently breaks the lookup.

t2p() failure is silent: the whole body is wrapped in one try whose catch (Exception) only calls e.printStackTrace(), the method returns void and rethrows nothing, so the action continues with the transient id-only object; ProductImageAction.delete documents the resulting org.hibernate.TransientObjectException when the redirect location later dereferences productImage.product.id.

Because t2p() replaces the action's field wholesale, a value bound onto the same object has to be read before the call: PropertyValueAction.update stashes propertyValue.getValue() in a local, calls t2p(propertyValue), then writes the local back onto the refreshed entity.

t2p() is called from 21 sites across the action classes, and it is not the only rebinding strategy: PropertyAction.update deliberately skips it because the bound Property already carries every field to write, and ProductAction.update re-reads the row only to copy the unchanged createDate onto the submitted object.

saveWithJpg(File) takes the target file as its parameter but reads the uploaded bytes off the inherited img field; its body is FileUtils.copyFile(img, file) followed by ImageUtil.change2jpg and ImageIO.write inside one try that catches IOException only, so it returns void and a write failure leaves the committed database row with no reliable file and only a stack trace as record.

The upload write path is asymmetric: CategoryAction.add calls saveWithJpg unconditionally after categoryService.save, while CategoryAction.update guards the same call with if (img != null), so a multipart submit that selects no file reaches FileUtils.copyFile with a null source - a failure that is not an IOException and therefore is not intercepted by the helper's catch.

Three call sites use saveWithJpg: CategoryAction.add, CategoryAction.update and ProductImageAction.add, the last one writing the two 56x56 and 217x190 derivatives through ImageUtil.resizeImage immediately afterwards.

Action4Service declares nine package-private interface-typed service fields - categoryService, propertyService, productService, productImageService, propertyValueService, userService, orderService, orderItemService, reviewService - each annotated @Autowired, and this one declaration is the only service access any of the 47 endpoint bodies has; no concrete action declares a service field of its own.

Service wiring in the action layer is by type, not by name: there is no @Qualifier, @Resource(name=...) or bean-name string in the action package, and each of the nine injected interfaces has exactly one implementation in com.caozhihu.tmall.service.impl (nine *ServiceImpl classes plus BaseServiceImpl and ServiceDelegateDAO).

Action4Service is the only @Component in the action package and declares no @Action method, while the concrete action classes carry no Spring stereotype; consequently the @Transactional(readOnly = false) on PropertyAction.add has no proxy to apply to, and the write is transactional only because propertyService.save carries its own annotation.

Because the nine services are injected as fields and BaseService is entity-agnostic, an action body can route a call through the wrong service without any compile error: ProductImageAction.delete deletes a ProductImage through propertyService.

The action layer consumes rather than declares business constants: action bodies reference OrderService.waitPay / waitDelivery / waitConfirm / waitReview / finish / delete and ProductImageService.type_single / type_detail, whose definitions belong to the service interfaces.

Endpoint bodies contain no exception handling: the only catch blocks in the whole action package are the two inside Action4Service (t2p and saveWithJpg), so an exception from a service call, a dereference or a reflection step escapes the method and the return statement that would name a result is never reached.

A result name returned by an action that no @Result declares cannot be resolved, and the failure occurs after the action body has already run, so any database write, file write or session attribute it performed stands; the repository declares no fallback or input result and no exception mapping anywhere.

Primitive fields on Action4Parameter (num, oiid, total, showonly) default to 0 or false when a request omits them while String and object fields stay null, which is why ForeAction.category guards its sorting switch with if (sort != null) and why a missing num yields a quantity of 0.

ForeAction.createOrder dereferences the session orderItems list with ois.isEmpty() before any null check, so a request made in a fresh session (no orderItems key) throws instead of reaching the intended login.jsp return.

Action instance fields are per-request scratch space: the only cross-request carriers an action body writes are the session attributes user and orderItems, and the redirect results re-send their inputs explicitly as OGNL-interpolated location parameters, which is necessary because the action's fields do not survive the 302.

Extension of the layer is narrow by construction: a new endpoint is one @Action method on a class extending Action4Result returning an existing or newly declared result name; a new bindable parameter is a field plus public setter on the appropriate chain class; a new service dependency is one more @Autowired field on Action4Service; and a new upload reuses the inherited img triple, since saveWithJpg hard-codes the img field as its source.
